blocks.label: string survival kit
blocks.code:
string s = "hello";
s.size();          // 5   (also s.length())
s[1] = 'E';        // hEllo — single char edits
s.substr(1, 3);    // "Ell" — start, COUNT
s.find("ll");      // 2 (index) or npos if absent
s += "!!";         // append
// compare with == : full content comparison (not addresses!)
blocks.py:
s = 'hello'
len(s)              # 5
s[1] = 'E'          # ERROR: strings immutable! Build new: s[:1]+'E'+s[2:]
s[1:4]              # 'ell' - start, END (not count!)
s.find('ll')        # 2 or -1 if absent
s += '!!'           # append
s == 'hello!!'      # content comparison

blocks.md: **Char arithmetic superpower:** `'A'`..`'Z'`, `'a'`..`'z'`, `'0'`..`'9'` are CONSECUTIVE codes. `ch - 'a'` gives 0..25 (alphabet slot); `ch - '0'` gives the digit value. Two idioms used forever.

items.title: Reverse String (in place)
items.statement: Reverse char vector without extra buffer.

solutionCode.label: two pointers swapping inward

items.complexity: n/2 swaps, one pass. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why does the problem hand you a char array rather than a string?
followups.a: In many languages strings are immutable, so "reverse in place" would be impossible — you would have to allocate. Passing a mutable array is what makes the O(1) space requirement meaningful rather than a trick question.

followups.q: Is this identical to reversing an int array?
followups.a: Yes, byte for byte. The element type never enters the algorithm — only the swap does. Recognising that a "string problem" is an array problem in disguise is most of what this module is teaching.

items.title: Valid Palindrome
hints: Skip non-alnum INSIDE loop before compare.

solutionCode.label: skip non-alphanumeric inside the loop, compare case-folded
solutionCode.py:
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
    while l < r:
        while l < r and not s[l].isalnum():   # skip junk from the left
            l += 1
        while l < r and not s[r].isalnum():   # and from the right
            r -= 1
        if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower():
            return False
        l += 1
        r -= 1
    return True

items.complexity: Time O(n), each character visited at most once by either pointer. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why does each inner skip loop need `l < r` as well?
followups.a: A string of only punctuation would otherwise run the pointer off the end. With ",,,," the left skip would walk past r and index out of bounds. The bound check is what makes "no valid characters at all" return true safely.

followups.q: Why cast to unsigned char before isalnum?
followups.a: In C++, passing a negative char to isalnum is undefined behaviour, and plain char is signed on most platforms — any byte above 127 becomes negative. The cast is not pedantry; it is the difference between correct and UB on non-ASCII input.

items.title: Valid Anagram (count array)
items.statement: Same letters same counts — 26-slot array version.

solutionCode.label: one array, incremented and decremented in the same pass

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) — 26 slots regardless of input length.

followups.q: Why is the length check not just an optimisation?
followups.a: Without it, "a" and "aa" would give counts of +1 then −2 in different slots — the loop only runs to the shorter length, so trailing characters are never seen. The guard is load-bearing, not a shortcut.

followups.q: Why one array instead of two?
followups.a: Two arrays need a comparison pass over both. One array with += and −= makes "equal" mean "all zeros", which is a single check. It also halves the memory traffic — a small thing here, but the same trick scales to large alphabets.

items.title: Jewels and Stones
hints: Set jewels; scan stones counting membership.

solutionCode.label: set the jewels, scan the stones

items.complexity: Time O(J + S). Space O(J) for the set.

followups.q: Why a set rather than scanning jewels for each stone?
followups.a: The nested scan is O(J·S). Hashing the jewels once turns each stone into an O(1) probe, giving O(J + S). With both strings at 50 characters it makes no practical difference — but the reflex matters when the sizes grow.

followups.q: Could you use a fixed array instead?
followups.a: Yes — jewels are letters, so a 128-slot bool array indexed by character code is faster than a hash set and needs no allocation. Bounded alphabet means an array beats a hash almost every time; the set is just more obviously correct at a glance.

items.title: Defanging an IP Address
hints: Append per char; dot → append four chars.

solutionCode.label: build a fresh string, expanding dots

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the result.

followups.q: Why build a new string rather than edit in place?
followups.a: The output is longer than the input — each dot becomes three characters. In-place editing would need to shift everything right for each dot, which is O(n) per dot and O(n²) overall. Appending to a fresh buffer is one linear pass.

followups.q: Why `reserve` in the C++ version?
followups.a: Without it, the string reallocates and copies as it grows — amortised O(n) but with several memcpys along the way. An IPv4 address has exactly three dots, so the final size is known: input + 6. Reserving makes it a single allocation.

items.title: Truncate Sentence
hints: Count spaces; cut after k-th word.

solutionCode.label: count spaces, cut after the k-th word

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) if you return a view, O(n) for a copy.

followups.q: Why count spaces rather than words?
followups.a: The k-th space is exactly the boundary after the k-th word, so the cut index falls out with no bookkeeping. Counting words means tracking transitions into and out of them — more state for the same answer. The problem guarantees single spaces and no leading or trailing space, which is what makes this valid.

followups.q: What if k equals the total word count?
followups.a: The loop never finds a k-th space, so it falls through and returns the whole string. That is correct — truncating to every word is the identity. Handling it by fallthrough rather than a special case is the cleaner shape.

items.title: Goal Parser Interpretation
hints: Peek TWO chars when current is '('.

solutionCode.label: peek the next character when you see an open paren

followups.q: Why is peeking `command[i+1]` safe here?
followups.a: The grammar guarantees that an open paren is always followed by at least one more character — "(" alone is not a valid token. Without that guarantee you would need a bounds check. State the guarantee out loud rather than relying on it silently.

followups.q: How would you generalise this to arbitrary token sets?
followups.a: A trie or a longest-match table keyed on the prefix, so you match the longest known token at each position rather than hardcoding lengths of 1, 2 and 4. That is how real tokenisers work, and it is the natural follow-up if the interviewer adds a third token.

items.title: First Palindrome in Array

solutionCode.label: reuse the two-pointer check, return the first hit

items.complexity: Time O(total characters) worst case. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why not use `w == reverse(w)`?
followups.a: It works and is one line, but it allocates a full reversed copy — O(n) extra space per word — and always scans the whole string even when the first pair already mismatches. The two-pointer version is O(1) space with early exit.

followups.q: Is the empty string a palindrome?
followups.a: Yes, vacuously — the loop never runs and returns true. Worth stating, because "" is also the sentinel for "none found" here, which makes an empty string in the input indistinguishable from failure. In production you would return an index or an optional instead.

items.title: Capitalize First Letter of Each Word

solutionCode.label: a flag that says whether the next character starts a word

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) if mutating in place.

followups.q: Why lowercase the non-first characters instead of leaving them?
followups.a: Title case means "hELLO wORLD" becomes "Hello World", not "HELLO WORLD". Leaving them alone only works if the input is already lowercase. Forcing the case makes the function idempotent — running it twice gives the same result.

followups.q: What breaks with multiple consecutive spaces?
followups.a: Nothing — each space re-sets the flag, so the next letter is still capitalised. That is the advantage of a flag over "capitalise index 0 and every index after a space", which double-counts on runs of spaces or breaks on leading whitespace.

items.title: Digit Sum of a String Number
items.statement: Sum digits inside mixed alphanumeric string.

solutionCode.label: guard with isdigit, convert by subtracting the zero character
solutionCode.py:
def digit_sum(s: str) -> int:
    return sum(int(c) for c in s if c.isdigit())

followups.q: Why does `c - '0'` give the numeric value?
followups.a: ASCII digit codes are consecutive: '0' is 48, '1' is 49, and so on. Subtracting the base gives the offset, which is the digit itself. It is the same trick as `c - 'a'` for alphabet indexing — one idiom, two uses.

followups.q: Why is the isdigit guard necessary rather than nice-to-have?
followups.a: Without it, a letter like 'a' (97) would contribute 97 − 48 = 49 to the sum. The function would silently return a plausible-looking wrong number rather than failing — the worst kind of bug.
